passages.title: Bangkok District Launches Free Evening Health Checks for Office Workers
paragraphs: Office workers in one of Bangkok's busiest business districts can now have their health checked on the way home. Since the beginning of this month, the district health centre has been offering free evening screening for blood pressure, blood sugar and body mass index (BMI) every Tuesday and Thursday from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m.

The service is aimed at employees who seldom see a doctor because most clinics have closed by the time they leave the office. According to the centre's director, Dr. Kittipong Srisuk, many people in their thirties and forties are unaware that they have high blood pressure or early-stage diabetes until the condition has already damaged their heart, kidneys or eyes. “These problems are often silent,” he explained. “A ten-minute check can reveal them years before any symptoms appear.”

No appointment is required, but participants are asked to bring their national ID card and to avoid eating for at least two hours beforehand so that the blood sugar reading is more accurate. Anyone whose results fall outside the normal range receives advice from a nurse and a referral letter to a nearby public hospital for further tests.

In the first two weeks, around 450 people took part. Nearly one in four of them had blood pressure above the recommended level, a proportion that staff had not anticipated. If demand keeps growing, the district intends to add Saturday sessions, and it is already encouraging large local companies to send employees in groups.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: A Bangkok district has started free after-work health checks for office employees.
Office workers in Bangkok are more likely than other people to develop diabetes.
A district health centre is asking companies to pay for their staff's medical tests.
Doctors warn that high blood pressure is now the most serious disease in Bangkok.

passages.title: Central Library Extends Opening Hours for the Final Examination Period
paragraphs: The Central Library is pleased to announce extended opening hours to support students during the final examination period. From Monday 17 November to Sunday 7 December, the library will be open from 8:00 a.m. to 2:00 a.m. every day, including weekends and public holidays. Normal opening hours (8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m.) will resume on Monday 8 December.

During the extended period, the ground and first floors will stay open until 2:00 a.m., while the second floor, which houses the print collection and the media room, will close at 10:00 p.m. as usual. Books may be borrowed or returned at the self-service machines on the ground floor whenever the building is open; however, the staffed service desk will operate only until 8:00 p.m.

Group study rooms can be reserved through the library website for up to three hours per person per day. Any room that has not been occupied within 15 minutes of the booking time will be released to other users. The silent study zone on the first floor is reserved for individual work, and mobile phone calls are not permitted in this area.

For safety reasons, entry after 10:00 p.m. is restricted to current students and staff, who must scan a valid university ID card at the entrance. Food may not be consumed in any reading area, although drinks in covered containers are permitted. A free shuttle bus will run between the library and the main dormitories every 30 minutes from 10:00 p.m. to 2:00 a.m.

Students who need help finding materials or searching online databases are encouraged to book a consultation with a subject librarian before Friday 14 November, as consultations will not be offered during the examination weeks. For further information, please contact the Library Information Desk.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of this notice?
options: to announce new rules on food and drink in the library
to explain why the library will close earlier once the exams are over
to inform users of longer opening hours and related arrangements
to encourage students to book group study rooms online

passages.title: Electric Motorcycles Gain Ground on Thai City Streets
paragraphs: On the crowded roads of Bangkok, Chiang Mai and Khon Kaen, a quieter kind of motorcycle is becoming a familiar sight. Electric motorcycles, once regarded as a novelty for wealthy enthusiasts, are now being bought by delivery riders, students and motorcycle-taxi drivers who want to cut their daily costs.

The appeal is largely financial. According to a 2024 survey of 800 delivery riders in three provinces, charging an electric motorcycle costs roughly one-fifth as much per kilometre as fuelling a comparable petrol model. Electric motors also contain far fewer moving parts, so they require less maintenance. “I used to change the oil every month,” said Anan, a food-delivery rider in Khon Kaen. “Now I hardly ever visit the repair shop.”

Environmental benefits are another selling point. Since they produce no exhaust, electric motorcycles do not directly add to the fine-particle (PM2.5) pollution that covers many Thai cities during the dry season. They are also considerably quieter, which residents of dense neighbourhoods welcome.

Nevertheless, several obstacles remain. The most frequently mentioned is the shortage of public charging points. Most owners charge their vehicles at home overnight, which is impractical for people living in rented rooms or condominiums without suitable power outlets. Battery-swapping stations, where riders can exchange an empty battery for a fully charged one in less than a minute, have opened in some districts, but they remain concentrated in city centres.

Cost is a further concern. Although running costs are low, the purchase price of an electric motorcycle is often higher than that of a similar petrol model, mainly because of the battery. Batteries also gradually lose capacity, and replacing one can cost almost half the price of the vehicle. As a result, some buyers hesitate, unsure whether the savings will outweigh the extra expense in the long run.

Industry analysts expect these barriers to shrink as battery prices fall and charging networks expand. For the time being, however, electric motorcycles remain a promising, though not yet perfect, answer to urban transport problems.

passages.title: Why We Forget — and How Spaced Repetition Helps Us Remember
paragraphs: Most students know the frustration of studying hard for a test, only to discover a week later that much of the material has disappeared. Yet forgetting is not necessarily a sign of laziness or poor ability. It is a normal function of the brain, which constantly filters incoming information so that it is not overloaded with details it may never need again.

The pattern of forgetting was first studied systematically in the 1880s by the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus. Acting as his own and only subject, he memorised lists of meaningless syllables and tested how many he could recall after different intervals. Memory declined steeply at first, with much of the material lost within a day, before the rate of loss slowed. Plotted on a graph, his results formed a sharply falling line that became known as the forgetting curve.

Ebbinghaus also made a second, more encouraging discovery. Each time he relearned a list, he needed less effort than before, and the information faded more slowly afterwards. In other words, each review seemed to flatten the curve. This observation forms the basis of a technique now known as spaced repetition.

Spaced repetition means reviewing material at gradually increasing intervals—for example, one day after first learning it, then three days later, then after a week and a month. Instead of cramming everything into one long session, learners return to the content just as they are starting to forget it. The effort of retrieving a fading memory appears to strengthen it far more than simply rereading notes.

The method has been tested in many settings. In one study at a university in northern Thailand, medical students who reviewed anatomy terms on a spaced schedule remembered considerably more after two months than classmates who spent the same total time studying in a single block. Similar benefits have been reported for foreign-language vocabulary and clinical guidelines.

Today, many flashcard apps use algorithms to decide when each item should be reviewed, showing difficult cards more often and easy ones less frequently. However, the principle does not depend on technology; a paper notebook and a simple calendar can serve the same purpose. What matters most is not the tool but the habit of returning to information before it slips away completely.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Students forget what they learn mainly because they do not study hard enough.
Forgetting is natural, but reviewing at increasing intervals improves memory.
Flashcard apps have become the most effective tool for learning new vocabulary.
Ebbinghaus showed that meaningless syllables are harder to learn than real words.
questions.explain: บทความเริ่มจาก ¶1: “forgetting is not necessarily a sign of laziness” แล้วอธิบายเส้นโค้งการลืมและวิธี spaced repetition จนจบ จึงตรงกับ B ตัวเลือก A ขัดกับ ¶1 โดยตรง ส่วน C และ D เป็นรายละเอียดย่อยหรือข้อสรุปที่บทความไม่ได้กล่าว

questions.q: According to paragraph 1, the brain forgets information partly in order to
options: recover after long periods of study
keep only the most recent information it receives
reduce stress before examinations
avoid being overloaded with unneeded details
questions.explain: ¶1: “constantly filters incoming information so that it is not overloaded with details it may never need again” สมองลืมเพื่อไม่ให้รับข้อมูลที่ไม่จำเป็นมากเกินไป ตัวเลือก B ฟังดูใกล้เคียงแต่บทความไม่ได้บอกว่าสมองเลือกเก็บเฉพาะข้อมูลล่าสุด

questions.q: The word 'steeply' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
options: sharply
slowly
steadily
unexpectedly
questions.explain: ¶2: “Memory declined steeply at first… before the rate of loss slowed” ความจำลดลงอย่างรวดเร็วและมากในช่วงแรกก่อนจะช้าลง ซึ่งสอดคล้องกับ “a sharply falling line” ตัวเลือก steadily ผิดเพราะหมายถึงสม่ำเสมอ ขัดกับการที่อัตราการลืมเปลี่ยนไป

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, what was unusual about Ebbinghaus's research?
options: He tested a large group of university medical students.
He used real words from several languages.
He was the only person who took part in it.
He recorded his results with a computer.
questions.explain: ¶2: “Acting as his own and only subject” Ebbinghaus ทดลองกับตัวเองเพียงคนเดียว ตัวเลือก A หลอกด้วยข้อมูลนักศึกษาแพทย์ซึ่งมาจากงานวิจัยใน ¶5 และ B ขัดกับข้อความที่ว่าเขาใช้ “meaningless syllables”

questions.q: What does 'This observation' in paragraph 3 refer to?
options: the finding that memory declines steeply at first
the finding that each review slowed later forgetting
the finding that meaningless syllables are easy to learn
the finding that relearning takes more effort over time
questions.explain: ¶3: “each time he relearned a list… the information faded more slowly afterwards. In other words, each review seemed to flatten the curve.” This observation จึงหมายถึงการทบทวนแต่ละครั้งทำให้ลืมช้าลง ตัวเลือก A คือข้อค้นพบแรกใน ¶2 ไม่ใช่ข้อสังเกตที่นำไปสู่ spaced repetition และ D กลับความหมาย

questions.q: What is the main purpose of paragraph 4?
options: to explain how spaced repetition is carried out
to report the results of a study on medical students
to compare several popular flashcard apps
to describe Ebbinghaus's early experiments
questions.explain: ¶4 เปิดด้วยนิยามและตัวอย่างตารางทบทวน: “Spaced repetition means reviewing material at gradually increasing intervals—for example, one day after…” จึงเป็นการอธิบายวิธีปฏิบัติ ตัวเลือก B เป็นหน้าที่ของ ¶5 และ D เป็นเนื้อหาของ ¶2–3

questions.q: It can be inferred from paragraph 4 that simply rereading notes
options: is the best preparation for an exam the next day
should be repeated at gradually increasing intervals
requires more effort than recalling information
is less effective than trying to recall information
questions.explain: ¶4: “The effort of retrieving a fading memory appears to strengthen it far more than simply rereading notes” จึงอนุมานได้ว่าการอ่านโน้ตซ้ำเฉย ๆ ได้ผลน้อยกว่าการพยายามดึงความจำออกมา ตัวเลือก C กลับด้าน เพราะบทความเน้นว่าการนึกให้ได้ต่างหากที่ต้องใช้ความพยายาม

questions.q: In the study described in paragraph 5, the two groups of students
options: studied different subjects at university
were tested after one week
spent the same total time studying
followed the same study schedule
questions.explain: ¶5: “classmates who spent the same total time studying in a single block” ทั้งสองกลุ่มใช้เวลารวมเท่ากัน ต่างกันที่การกระจายเวลา ตัวเลือก D ผิดเพราะกลุ่มหนึ่งใช้ตารางแบบเว้นระยะ อีกกลุ่มอ่านรวดเดียว และ B ผิดเพราะทดสอบหลังสองเดือน

questions.q: Why does the author mention 'a paper notebook and a simple calendar' in paragraph 6?
options: to show that the method can work without technology
to suggest that flashcard apps are often unreliable
to recommend products that students should buy
to explain how algorithms choose review times
questions.explain: ¶6: “the principle does not depend on technology; a paper notebook and a simple calendar can serve the same purpose” ผู้เขียนยกตัวอย่างนี้เพื่อแสดงว่าใช้วิธีนี้ได้โดยไม่ต้องพึ่งแอป ตัวเลือก B ผิดเพราะบทความไม่ได้วิจารณ์ว่าแอปไม่น่าเชื่อถือ

questions.q: How is the information in the passage organised?
options: Two competing theories of memory are presented and then compared.
A common problem is explained, then research and a practical method follow.
Major events in the history of psychology are listed in time order.
An argument against using technology for learning is supported with examples.
questions.explain: ¶1 เสนอปัญหาการลืม ¶2–3 เป็นงานวิจัยของ Ebbinghaus ¶4–6 อธิบายวิธี spaced repetition หลักฐาน และการนำไปใช้ จึงเป็นโครงสร้าง ปัญหา–งานวิจัย–วิธีแก้ ตัวเลือก D ผิดเพราะ ¶6 ไม่ได้คัดค้านเทคโนโลยี เพียงบอกว่าไม่จำเป็นต้องใช้

passages.title: Rising Waistlines: The Drivers of Obesity in Southeast Asia and the Policy Response
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, obesity was regarded as a problem of wealthy Western nations. In Southeast Asia, public health programmes concentrated instead on undernutrition, infectious disease and maternal and child health. Over the past three decades, however, this picture has changed dramatically. Rates of overweight and obesity have climbed across the region, often while undernutrition persists in poorer communities. The coexistence of these two problems, sometimes within a single household, is known as the double burden of malnutrition, and it confronts health systems with an unusually complex challenge.

The scale of the increase is striking. A 2022 review of national health surveys from six Southeast Asian countries estimated that the proportion of adults classified as overweight had roughly doubled over twenty years in several of them. Among children and adolescents the rise was proportionally even steeper, a trend that alarms researchers because overweight children frequently remain overweight as adults. The consequences extend far beyond appearance. Excess body weight is a major risk factor for type 2 diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease and several cancers—conditions that are costly to treat and that place long-term pressure on public budgets.

Researchers commonly explain this trend through the concept of the nutrition transition. As incomes rise, diets tend to move away from traditional patterns based on rice, vegetables, legumes and fish towards foods that are higher in refined carbohydrates, added sugar, salt and saturated fat. In Southeast Asia, this shift has been accelerated by the rapid spread of convenience stores and fast-food chains, which make inexpensive, energy-dense products available at almost any hour. Sweetened beverages deserve particular attention. Sugary teas, coffees and soft drinks are now part of the daily routine of many young people, and because liquid calories produce only a weak feeling of fullness, they are easily consumed on top of regular meals.

Urbanisation has reinforced these dietary changes. Millions of people have migrated from rural villages to cities such as Bangkok, Jakarta, Manila and Ho Chi Minh City in search of work. Urban residents typically face long working hours and lengthy commutes, which leave little time to prepare meals at home. Instead, they rely on street food, ready-made meals and, increasingly, food-delivery applications. While street food can be nutritious, portion sizes have grown, and many popular dishes are deep-fried or served with sweet sauces. Moreover, city dwellers are surrounded by advertising for snacks and soft drinks, much of it aimed deliberately at children.

At the same time, levels of physical activity have fallen. Agricultural and manual work, which once demanded considerable energy, has been replaced for many people by office and service jobs that involve sitting for most of the day. Motorised transport has largely displaced walking and cycling, partly because of the hot climate and partly because many cities lack shaded pavements and safe cycle lanes. Children, too, are less active than previous generations. Intense academic competition means that many spend their evenings and weekends at tutoring schools, leaving limited time for sport or outdoor play, while screen-based entertainment fills much of what remains.

Governments in the region have begun to respond, and fiscal measures have attracted the most attention. Thailand introduced a tiered excise tax on sugar-sweetened beverages in 2017, under which drinks with a higher sugar content are taxed at higher rates, and several neighbouring countries have since adopted comparable schemes. The design of such taxes matters. Because the rate depends on sugar content rather than on volume, manufacturers have a strong incentive to change their recipes. Evaluations suggest that this is precisely what happened: rather than simply passing higher prices on to consumers, many manufacturers reformulated their drinks to qualify for lower tax bands. Critics argue that such taxes fall most heavily on low-income households, although supporters reply that these households also bear the greatest burden of diet-related disease.

A second group of measures aims to help consumers make better choices. Front-of-pack labels, such as simple logos identifying healthier products or colour-coded grades showing sugar content, allow shoppers to compare items at a glance instead of studying detailed nutrition tables. Schools have also become an important setting for intervention. Programmes in several countries restrict the sale of sugary drinks and fried snacks on school grounds, provide healthier lunches and require a fixed period of daily physical activity. However, their impact is frequently weakened by inconsistent enforcement and by vendors who sell unhealthy food outside school gates, beyond the reach of school rules.

No single measure is likely to reverse the rise in obesity on its own. Taxes, labels and school programmes each address only one part of a problem that is rooted in economic development, urban design and changing social norms. Arguably, the most promising strategies are those that make the healthy choice the easy choice—for example, by improving access to affordable fresh food, designing walkable neighbourhoods and protecting children from aggressive marketing—rather than relying mainly on individual willpower. Achieving this will require health ministries to work closely with sectors such as transport, education, agriculture and commerce.

questions.q: Which of the following is the best title for the passage?
options: The Success of Sugar Taxes in Thailand and Its Neighbours
Obesity in Southeast Asia: Causes and Policy Responses
Why Children in Asian Cities No Longer Play Outdoors
Undernutrition: Southeast Asia's Forgotten Health Crisis
questions.explain: บทความอธิบายสาเหตุของโรคอ้วน (¶3–5) และมาตรการของรัฐ (¶6–7: “Governments in the region have begun to respond”) ชื่อเรื่อง B จึงครอบคลุมที่สุด ตัวเลือก A แคบเกินไปเพราะภาษีน้ำตาลเป็นเพียงมาตรการเดียวใน ¶6 และ D ผิดเพราะภาวะทุพโภชนาการถูกกล่าวถึงเพียงในบทนำ

questions.q: According to paragraph 1, public health programmes in twentieth-century Southeast Asia mainly focused on
options: reducing obesity in wealthy families
treating heart disease and diabetes
undernutrition and infectious disease
controlling food advertising to children
questions.explain: ¶1: “public health programmes concentrated instead on undernutrition, infectious disease and maternal and child health” ตัวเลือก A หลอกด้วยประโยคแรกที่บอกว่าโรคอ้วนเคยถูกมองว่าเป็นปัญหาของ “wealthy Western nations” ไม่ใช่สิ่งที่โครงการในภูมิภาคนี้เน้น

questions.q: The word 'striking' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
options: remarkable
violent
uncertain
gradual
questions.explain: ¶2: “The scale of the increase is striking.” ตามด้วยตัวเลขที่เพิ่มขึ้นเกือบเท่าตัว คำนี้จึงหมายถึง “น่าทึ่ง/เด่นชัด” ตัวเลือก violent มาจากความหมายของกริยา strike (ตี) ซึ่งไม่เข้ากับบริบท และ gradual ขัดกับการเพิ่มขึ้นอย่างรวดเร็ว

questions.q: It can be inferred from paragraph 2 that rising obesity among children is particularly worrying because
options: the treatment of children is far more expensive than that of adults
it has already doubled in all six of the countries studied
overweight children usually lose weight as they grow up
it is likely to increase diet-related disease among future adults
questions.explain: ¶2: “overweight children frequently remain overweight as adults” เมื่อรวมกับข้อมูลว่าน้ำหนักเกินเป็นปัจจัยเสี่ยงของเบาหวานและโรคหัวใจ จึงอนุมานได้ว่าจะมีผู้ใหญ่ป่วยโรคเหล่านี้มากขึ้นในอนาคต ตัวเลือก B อ่านตัวเลขผิด เพราะ “roughly doubled” พูดถึงผู้ใหญ่ “in several of them” ไม่ใช่เด็กในทุกประเทศ

questions.q: The word 'accelerated' in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to
options: reversed
sped up
started
measured
questions.explain: ¶3: “this shift has been accelerated by the rapid spread of convenience stores and fast-food chains” ร้านสะดวกซื้อทำให้การเปลี่ยนแปลงที่เกิดจากรายได้สูงขึ้น “เร็วขึ้น” ตัวเลือก started น่าหลง แต่ย่อหน้าบอกว่าการเปลี่ยนแปลงเริ่มจากรายได้ที่เพิ่มขึ้นอยู่แล้ว ร้านค้าเพียงเร่งให้เร็วขึ้น

questions.q: According to paragraph 3, sweetened drinks are a particular concern because they
options: do not make people feel full, so they are added to normal meals
are more expensive than traditional foods such as rice and fish
contain more salt than most fast-food products
are sold only in convenience stores and fast-food chains
questions.explain: ¶3: “because liquid calories produce only a weak feeling of fullness, they are easily consumed on top of regular meals” ตัวเลือก D ใช้คำที่ปรากฏในย่อหน้า (convenience stores) มาหลอก แต่บทความไม่ได้บอกว่าเครื่องดื่มหวานขายเฉพาะที่นั่น

the growing use of food-delivery apps

They describe one main cause and two of its effects.

questions.q: It can be inferred from paragraph 5 that shaded pavements and safe cycle lanes might

encourage more people to walk or cycle
make the region's hot climate cooler
increase the use of motorised transport

to argue that the tax should be based on volume instead

front-of-pack labels
shoppers
vendors outside schools

questions.q: Which of the following statements from the passage expresses an opinion rather than a fact?

Millions of people have migrated from rural villages to cities in search of work.
Arguably, the most promising strategies are those that make the healthy choice the easy choice.
Excess body weight is a major risk factor for type 2 diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease and several cancers.

questions.q: What concept do researchers use to explain the shift from traditional diets to foods high in sugar and fat? (Answer in NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS from the passage.)

questions.q: According to paragraph 6, what did many manufacturers do instead of simply passing higher prices on to consumers? (Answer in NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶6: “rather than simply passing higher prices on to consumers, many manufacturers reformulated their drinks to qualify for lower tax bands” คือปรับสูตรเครื่องดื่มให้น้ำตาลน้อยลงเพื่อเสียภาษีในอัตราที่ต่ำกว่า

questions.explain: ¶7: “vendors who sell unhealthy food outside school gates, beyond the reach of school rules” การขายนอกรั้วโรงเรียนทำให้กฎของโรงเรียนควบคุมไม่ได้ และทำให้ผลของโครงการลดลง

passages.title: Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging: Promise, Pitfalls and the Continuing Role of the Clinician
paragraphs: Medical imaging—including X-rays, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and ultrasound—lies at the heart of modern diagnosis. Yet in many countries the number of images produced each year is growing far faster than the number of radiologists trained to interpret them. The result is heavy workloads, fatigue and, in some hospitals, delays of days or even weeks before a scan is reported. Against this background, artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely promoted as a way of easing the pressure on imaging services.

Most current systems rely on a technique known as deep learning. Rather than following explicit rules written by programmers, a deep learning model learns from large collections of labelled examples. If it is shown many thousands of chest X-rays that specialists have classified as either normal or showing pneumonia, for instance, the model gradually adjusts millions of internal parameters until it can distinguish between the two categories on its own. This sets it apart from earlier computer-aided detection software, which depended on hand-coded instructions and often produced so many false alarms that radiologists learned to ignore it.

In carefully controlled studies, the results have been impressive. Algorithms have matched experienced specialists in a number of narrowly defined tasks, such as detecting signs of diabetic eye disease in retinal photographs, identifying small lung nodules on CT scans and spotting fractures on X-rays. AI can also be used for triage: by flagging scans that appear to show an urgent problem, such as bleeding in the brain, it allows radiologists to examine those cases first. At one large teaching hospital in Southeast Asia, a 2023 audit found that introducing such a system cut the average time taken to report urgent head scans by almost half.

The potential benefits are greatest where specialists are scarce. In rural areas of Thailand and several other countries, AI tools have been tested for diabetic eye screening: a nurse photographs the patient's retina, and the software returns a result within minutes, so that patients who need treatment can be referred on the same day instead of waiting weeks for a specialist's report. However, field trials have also exposed practical difficulties. Poor lighting in some clinics produced images that the system rejected as unreadable, and unstable internet connections repeatedly interrupted the uploading of photographs, forcing patients to return another day.

A more fundamental limitation concerns generalisability. An algorithm trained on images from one hospital may perform noticeably worse at another because of differences in scanner models, imaging protocols and patient populations, a problem known as dataset shift. In one widely discussed case, a model designed to detect pneumonia on chest X-rays appeared highly accurate, but further analysis suggested that it was partly relying on features unrelated to the disease, such as markings that revealed which hospital an image had come from. Similarly, if certain groups, such as particular ethnic groups or age ranges, are underrepresented in the training data, the system may perform less reliably for those patients.

Two further concerns relate to the way humans interact with these systems. First, many deep learning models function as a 'black box', producing an answer without revealing the reasoning behind it. Colour-coded 'heat maps', which highlight the regions of an image that most influenced a decision, offer some insight but can themselves be misleading. Second, clinicians may come to trust the software too readily, a tendency known as automation bias. In a 2023 experiment involving 27 radiologists, participants who were shown deliberately incorrect AI suggestions made noticeably more errors than when they read the same images without assistance.

These problems explain why experts insist on rigorous validation before AI tools are used in routine care. An algorithm should be tested not only on data from the institution where it was developed but also on images from other hospitals, a process called external validation. Ideally, it should then be evaluated prospectively, within real clinical workflows, rather than only on stored images. Even after deployment, ongoing monitoring is essential, since performance can drift as equipment, software and patient populations change. Regulatory approval is an important step, but it does not guarantee that a system will perform equally well in every setting.

None of this means that AI has failed to deliver. About a decade ago, some commentators predicted that radiologists would soon be unnecessary; instead, demand for their expertise has continued to rise. A more realistic vision is one of augmented practice, in which software handles repetitive tasks such as measuring lesions and prioritising worklists, while clinicians integrate imaging findings with the patient's history, discuss uncertain cases with colleagues and take responsibility for the final decision. The central question is therefore no longer whether AI will be used in medical imaging, but how it can be used safely, fairly and transparently.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: AI has already replaced radiologists in many large hospitals.
Deep learning systems are less accurate than older computer-aided detection.
AI is useful mainly in rural clinics where specialists are scarce.
AI can improve imaging, but it requires validation and human oversight.
questions.explain: บทความกล่าวถึงประโยชน์ (¶3–4) ข้อจำกัด (¶5–6) และความจำเป็นของการตรวจสอบและบทบาทแพทย์ (¶7–8: “take responsibility for the final decision”) จึงตรงกับ D ตัวเลือก A ขัดกับ ¶8 ที่บอกว่าความต้องการรังสีแพทย์ยังเพิ่มขึ้น และ C แคบเกินไปเพราะเป็นเพียงเนื้อหาของ ¶4

questions.q: According to paragraph 1, what has created interest in using AI for medical imaging?
options: Image numbers are rising faster than radiologist numbers.
Patients increasingly prefer computers to human doctors.
New types of scanner produce images that humans cannot interpret.
Radiologists have asked for software that can replace them.
questions.explain: ¶1: “the number of images produced each year is growing far faster than the number of radiologists trained to interpret them” ทำให้งานล้นมือและรายงานผลล่าช้า AI จึงถูกเสนอเป็นทางออก ตัวเลือก C หลอกด้วยคำว่า interpret แต่บทความไม่ได้บอกว่ามนุษย์อ่านภาพไม่ได้ เพียงแต่มีรังสีแพทย์ไม่พอ

questions.q: The word 'explicit' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
options: very complicated
hidden
clearly stated
temporary
questions.explain: ¶2: “Rather than following explicit rules written by programmers” กฎที่โปรแกรมเมอร์เขียนไว้ชัดเจนเป็นข้อ ๆ ตรงข้ามกับการที่โมเดลเรียนรู้รูปแบบเองจากตัวอย่าง จึงหมายถึง clearly stated ส่วน hidden มีความหมายตรงข้าม

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, how do deep learning systems differ from earlier computer-aided detection software?
options: They need no examples in order to learn.
They learn from labelled examples instead of hand-coded rules.
They tend to produce many more false alarms than the earlier software did.
They are designed so that radiologists can safely ignore them.
questions.explain: ¶2: deep learning “learns from large collections of labelled examples” ขณะที่ซอฟต์แวร์รุ่นก่อน “depended on hand-coded instructions” ตัวเลือก C กลับด้าน เพราะซอฟต์แวร์รุ่นเก่าต่างหากที่แจ้งเตือนผิดบ่อยจนรังสีแพทย์ไม่สนใจ

questions.q: Why does the author mention 'bleeding in the brain' in paragraph 3?
options: to give an example of a case that AI can help doctors prioritise
to show that AI is not yet able to detect serious brain injuries reliably
to compare the accuracy of CT scans with that of X-rays
to explain why radiologists often feel tired at work
questions.explain: ¶3: “by flagging scans that appear to show an urgent problem, such as bleeding in the brain, it allows radiologists to examine those cases first” เลือดออกในสมองเป็นตัวอย่างของภาวะเร่งด่วนที่ AI ช่วยจัดลำดับให้อ่านก่อน ตัวเลือก B ขัดกับย่อหน้าที่รายงานผลเชิงบวก

questions.q: The word 'scarce' in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to
options: very expensive to employ
highly trained
unwilling
in short supply
questions.explain: ¶4: “The potential benefits are greatest where specialists are scarce.” ตัวอย่างที่ตามมาคือพื้นที่ชนบทที่ผู้ป่วยต้องรอรายงานจากแพทย์เฉพาะทางหลายสัปดาห์ แสดงว่ามีแพทย์เฉพาะทางน้อย ตัวเลือก very expensive to employ ฟังดูเป็นไปได้แต่บริบทพูดถึงจำนวน ไม่ใช่ค่าจ้าง

questions.q: The problems found in the field trials described in paragraph 4 suggest that
options: nurses are not able to take clear retinal photographs
AI tools should also be tested in real clinical conditions
rural patients are generally unwilling to be screened by a computer
internet connections in large cities are generally unreliable
questions.explain: ¶4: “field trials have also exposed practical difficulties” เช่น แสงไม่พอและอินเทอร์เน็ตไม่เสถียร ซึ่งไม่ปรากฏในการศึกษาแบบควบคุม (¶3) จึงอนุมานได้ว่าต้องทดสอบ AI ในสภาพการทำงานจริงด้วย ตัวเลือก A ผิดเพราะภาพใช้ไม่ได้เนื่องจาก “Poor lighting” ไม่ใช่ความสามารถของพยาบาล

questions.q: It can be inferred from the pneumonia example in paragraph 5 that the model
options: was more accurate than human radiologists
had been trained on far too few chest X-ray images
might perform poorly on images from other hospitals
could clearly explain the reasons for its decisions
questions.explain: ¶5: โมเดลอาศัย “markings that revealed which hospital an image had come from” แทนลักษณะของโรค เมื่อนำไปใช้กับภาพจากโรงพยาบาลที่ไม่มีเครื่องหมายเหล่านั้น ความแม่นยำจึงน่าจะลดลง ตัวเลือก A ผิดเพราะความแม่นยำที่เห็นเป็นเพียง “appeared highly accurate” ซึ่งภายหลังพบว่าไม่น่าเชื่อถือ

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in paragraph 5 as a reason why an algorithm may perform worse at a new hospital?
options: differences in scanner models
differences in imaging protocols
differences in patient populations
differences in radiologist numbers
questions.explain: ¶5: “because of differences in scanner models, imaging protocols and patient populations” ไม่มีการกล่าวถึงจำนวนรังสีแพทย์ในย่อหน้านี้ ตัวเลือก D หลอกเพราะการขาดแคลนรังสีแพทย์ปรากฏใน ¶1 แต่เป็นเหตุผลที่ทำให้สนใจ AI ไม่ใช่สาเหตุที่อัลกอริทึมทำงานแย่ลง

questions.q: What does 'they' in paragraph 6 refer to?
options: the radiologists in the experiment
the deliberately incorrect AI suggestions
the colour-coded heat maps
the deep learning models
questions.explain: ¶6: “participants who were shown deliberately incorrect AI suggestions made noticeably more errors than when they read the same images” ผู้ที่อ่านภาพคือผู้เข้าร่วมการทดลองซึ่งเป็นรังสีแพทย์ 27 คน ตัวเลือก B อยู่ใกล้คำว่า they ที่สุดแต่คำแนะนำของ AI ไม่สามารถ “read” ภาพได้

questions.q: Which of the following statements from the passage is an opinion rather than a fact?
options: Most current systems rely on a technique known as deep learning.
A more realistic vision is one of augmented practice.
Algorithms have matched experienced specialists in a number of narrowly defined tasks.
In a 2023 experiment involving 27 radiologists, participants made noticeably more errors.
questions.explain: ¶8: “A more realistic vision is one of augmented practice” คำว่า more realistic เป็นการประเมินของผู้เขียนว่าภาพอนาคตแบบใดสมเหตุสมผลกว่า ส่วนตัวเลือกอื่นเป็นข้อมูลที่ตรวจสอบได้จากงานวิจัย เช่น ตัวเลือก D รายงานผลการทดลองที่ระบุปีและจำนวนผู้เข้าร่วม

questions.q: The author's attitude toward the use of AI in medical imaging can best be described as
options: hostile and suspicious
excited and uncritical
balanced but broadly positive
detached and largely uninterested
questions.explain: ¶8: “None of this means that AI has failed to deliver.” ผู้เขียนยอมรับประโยชน์ของ AI แต่ก็ใช้หลายย่อหน้า (¶5–7) อธิบายข้อจำกัดและความจำเป็นในการตรวจสอบ จึงเป็นทัศนคติที่สมดุลแต่ค่อนไปทางบวก ตัวเลือก B ผิดเพราะผู้เขียนไม่ได้มองข้ามความเสี่ยง

questions.q: What technique do most current AI imaging systems rely on? (Answer in NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶2: “Most current systems rely on a technique known as deep learning.” ซึ่งเป็นการเรียนรู้จากตัวอย่างภาพที่มีป้ายกำกับจำนวนมาก

questions.q: In the rural eye-screening programmes, who takes the photograph of the patient's retina? (Answer in NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶4: “a nurse photographs the patient's retina, and the software returns a result within minutes” ผู้ถ่ายภาพจึงเป็นพยาบาล ไม่ใช่จักษุแพทย์ ซึ่งช่วยให้คัดกรองได้ในพื้นที่ที่ขาดแพทย์เฉพาะทาง

questions.q: What name is given to the problem of an algorithm performing worse on images from a different hospital? (Answer in NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶5: “An algorithm trained on images from one hospital may perform noticeably worse at another… a problem known as dataset shift”

questions.q: What term describes the tendency of clinicians to rely on AI software more than they should? (Answer in NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶6: “clinicians may come to trust the software too readily, a tendency known as automation bias” โจทย์ถอดความ trust too readily เป็น rely on… more than they should

questions.q: According to paragraph 7, what remains essential even after an AI system has been deployed? (Answer in NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶7: “Even after deployment, ongoing monitoring is essential, since performance can drift” เพราะประสิทธิภาพอาจเปลี่ยนไปเมื่ออุปกรณ์ ซอฟต์แวร์ หรือกลุ่มผู้ป่วยเปลี่ยน
